where many copies have Διός [of Zeus], which would be acceptable, unless it could be doubted whether Aeschylus wrote καὶ προσδοκᾶν χρὴ Ζηνὶ δεσπόσειν τινά [and one must expect that someone will rule over Zeus], lest the verse be composed of three equal parts, with the verb δεσπόζειν [to rule] constructed with the dative, as ἄρχειν [to rule] is sometimes constructed with the dative and was constructed by Aeschylus himself in this play at line 945 δαρόν γὰρ οὐκ ἄρξει θεοῖς [for he will not rule the gods for long], and likewise ἐπιδεσπόζειν [to rule over] in Persians 241 τίς δὲ ποιμάνωρ ἔπεστι κἀπιδεσπόζει στρατῷ [who is the shepherd-commander who is in charge and rules over the army?]; where there is no reason why the dative στρατῷ [the army] (changed in many copies to στρατοῦ [of the army]) should be thought to be used because of the preceding verb ἔπεστι [is in charge].
